title: WIIZARD
description: Old Wiis turned into garage arcade cabinets on CRT TVs. They boot straight into WIIZARD, a launcher I designed and built, with an attract mode, collections and one-button starts for arcade, console, GameCube and Wii games. No menus, no settings, no Wii Remote.

modules.html:
An arcade anyone can walk up to

A softmodded Wii can play almost anything, but getting to a game means the Wii Menu, the Homebrew Channel, a loader and a Wii Remote. That's fine for me and hopeless for a kid in the garage. I wanted each cabinet to feel like a real arcade machine: turn it on, see something playing, press a button, play.

So every cabinet boots straight into WIIZARD. It plays gameplay clips in attract mode until someone picks up a pad, then shows a browse menu with collections like Quick Picks, Little Kids and Arcade Classics. Arcade sets, console classics, GameCube discs and Wii games all start the same way, with one button.

modules.html:
Designed to be kid-proof

  • Nothing to break. Reset and HOME always go back to attract mode, never out of the launcher. There's no path to a settings screen.
  • One way out of every game. L + R + Z + Start exits any arcade or GameCube game, and the loading screen shows it, along with that game's controls.
  • No accidental presses. Buttons do nothing for 0.8 seconds after a screen changes, so a mashed button doesn't skip what you were about to see.
  • It recovers on its own. A game that doesn't start is retried once, then shows a plain message. One that fails twice is hidden and flagged for me.
  • Made for the TV it's on. Each CRT is calibrated for width, height and position, and games run at their original 240p resolution so pixels look right.

A look that reads across a garage

The art direction is a maximal collage: pink halftone paper, cut blue and yellow shapes, and the selected game's clip on a taped, tilted photo. It reads from across a garage and feels like a toy, not a settings app.

The wizard is my own character. I cut him out of the original Photoshop file and puppeted him for the power-on intro: a pop-in with squash and stretch, a blink, the Wii Remote flicked up like a wand, and a wink.

modules.html:
Built for real hardware

I built the launcher in C for the Wii with its own graphics code, after the off-the-shelf renderer crashed. It runs the menu at 60 fps on a 2006 console. A small agent inside it lets me run the whole fleet from a Mac, hands-free, with Claude through an MCP server: screenshots, button presses, installs and updates.

The first cabinet sits next to the router but its USB network adapter wasn't one the Wii supports. So I wrote a driver for it, with a full network stack on top. As far as I know it's the only public homebrew USB Ethernet driver for the Wii, and I've packaged it as its own library, libwiieth.

Designed from what gets played

Every cabinet reports what gets played and what fails. Collections are ordered by what actually gets played, updates download on their own while the cabinet sits in attract mode, and a nightly report tells me which cabinet needs attention.
